source_text: Se de hoc satis sit, nunc quae sequuntur arripiam. In corpore igitur mortis huius, quale in paradiso ante peccatum, profecto non erat, alia lex in membris nostris repugnat legi mentis; quia et quando nolumus, et quando non consentimus, nec ei membra nostra ut impleat quod appetit exhibemus; habitat tamen in eis, et mentem resistentem repugnantemque sollicitat; ut ipse conflictus etiamsi non sit damnabilis, quia non perficit iniquitatem; sit tamen misera lis, quia non habet pacem [n165] . Naturalem esse omnium sensuum voluptatem, testimonio universitatis docemus. Hanc autem voluptatem et concupiscentiam ante peccatum in paradiso fuisse, res illa declarat, quia ad delictum via per concupiscentiam fuit, quae cum pomi decore oculos incitasset, spem etiam iucundi irritavit saporis. Non ergo potuit haec concupiscentia, quae cum modum non tenet, peccat; cum vero intra limitem concessorum tenetur, affectio naturalis et innocens est; non, inquam, potuit fructus esse peccati, quae docetur, non suo quidem vitio, sed voluntatis, occasio fuisse peccati. Lege et de hoc secundum librum meum: invenies hoc quod dicimus etiam tuo posse animo persuaderi. Quod vero quasi acutule posuisti, legem quidem peccati esse in membris nostris; sed tunc habere peccatum, quando ei consentimus; tunc vero solum proelium suscitare, quando non consentimus, et indicere miseriam pace turbata; quis non prudens pugnare perspiciat? Nam si lex peccati, id est, peccatum, et necessitas peccati membris est inserta naturaliter; quid prodest non ei praebere consensum, cum propter hoc ipsum quod est, necesse sit subire supplicium? Aut si est lex quidem peccati, sed quando ei non consentio non peccat; inaestimabilis potentia voluntatis humanae, quae (si dici permittat absurditas) cogit ipsum non peccare peccatum. Sed revertitur eo, ut quod dicis asystaton sit; nam si non peccat, nec lex peccati est; si lex peccati est, peccat; si vero peccat, solum quia est, quomodo ei obsisti potest ut non peccetur, quae repelli non potest ut a peccati opere desinatur?
pass_a_gloss: But let this be enough about this; now I will snatch those things which follow. In the body therefore of this death, such as in paradise before sin certainly was not, another law in our members fights the law of the mind; because both when we are unwilling, and when we do not consent, nor do we exhibit our members to it that it may fulfill what it seeks; nevertheless it dwells in them, and solicits the resisting and fighting mind; so that the conflict itself, even if it is not damnable, because it does not complete iniquity; is nevertheless miserable, because it does not have peace. That the pleasure of all senses is natural, we teach by the testimony of the universe. But that this pleasure and concupiscence were in paradise before sin, that thing declares, because the way to the fault was through concupiscence, which when it had stirred the eyes by the beauty of the fruit, also irritated the hope of a pleasant taste. This concupiscence therefore could not, which when it does not hold the measure, sins; but when it is held within the limit of things conceded, is a natural and innocent affection; it could not, I say, be a fruit of sin, which is taught to have been an occasion of sin, not by its own vice indeed, but of the will. Read also about this my second book: you will find that this which we say can be persuaded even to your mind. But what you placed as if somewhat sharply, that there is indeed a law of sin in our members; but then it has sin, when we consent to it; but then only it raises a battle, when we do not consent, and declares misery with peace disturbed; who being prudent would not see that it fights? For if the law of sin, that is, sin, and the necessity of sin has been inserted naturally in the members; what does it profit not to offer consent to it, when on account of this itself that it is, it is necessary to undergo punishment? Or if it is indeed a law of sin, but when I do not consent to it it does not sin; an inestimable power of the human will, which (if absurdity would permit it to be said) forces sin itself not to sin. But it returns to this, that what you say is asystaton; for if it does not sin, neither is it a law of sin; if it is a law of sin, it sins; but if it sins, only because it is, how can it be stood against so that it is not sinned, which cannot be driven back so that it cease from the work of sin?

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: But enough of this; I will now take up what follows. “In the body of this death, then, a body such as certainly did not exist in paradise before sin, another law in our members fights against the law of our mind. Even when we do not will it, do not consent to it, and do not offer our members for it to accomplish what it desires, it nevertheless dwells in them and troubles the mind that resists and fights back. Even if the conflict itself does not merit condemnation, because it does not carry out injustice, it is still a miserable struggle because it has no peace” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.6; compare Romans 7:23).

The universal testimony of humanity teaches us that the pleasure of all the senses is natural. That this pleasure and desire existed in paradise before sin is shown by the fact that desire was the route to the offense. After the fruit's beauty excited the eyes, it also stirred up the hope of a pleasant taste (Genesis 3:6). This desire sins when it fails to keep its proper measure, but when it stays within the bounds of what is allowed, it is a natural and innocent feeling. It cannot, I say, have been a fruit of sin when it is shown to have been an occasion of sin, not through its own fault but through the will's. Read my second book on this too; you will find that what we say can convince even your mind.

As for the supposedly clever distinction you made, that the law of sin is indeed in our members but involves sin only when we consent to it, while when we do not consent it merely starts a battle and inflicts misery by disturbing peace, what sensible person would not see the contradiction? If the law of sin, that is, sin and the necessity of sin, is naturally implanted in our members, what good is it not to consent to it, when one must undergo punishment simply because it exists? Or if it is indeed the law of sin but does not sin when I do not consent to it, then the human will has an immeasurable power: if the absurdity may be uttered, it forces sin itself not to sin! But we return to the fact that your statement cannot hold together. If it does not sin, it is not the law of sin. If it is the law of sin, it sins. And if it sins simply by existing, how can one resist it so that sin does not occur, when it cannot be driven away so that sin's activity may cease?

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
